description: We're drawn to Earth observation challenges, especially ones with a real story here in Malaysia and Southeast Asia, such as haze, floods and a changing climate.
summary:
Fire Harmony is one consistent worldwide fire record from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, from November 2000 to October 2026, and a free web app built on it. The two sensors see fire very differently: VIIRS counts about six times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fires, so a simple join makes a fake 8.4-fold jump in 2012. We put every satellite on the NOAA-20 VIIRS scale with a machine learning model trained on the years both flew, and give every value a 90% range. On years and regions the model never saw, 92% to 96% of monthly totals fall inside that range, and at both sensor changes the record steps by less than 1%.

In the app, anyone can pick a country, state, city or drawn area and any range of months, on a laptop or a phone. They get a burning calendar, how unusual a month is, tested trends, why a month was unusual, a three month outlook, rankings of 4,330 places, the link between fires and haze in Southeast Asia, an AI assistant, and every hotspot to download. Fire managers can now compare a season with 26 years of history on one scale.
details:
Try it:

· The live app, free and with no login: https://warren-530.github.io/fire-harmony/

· Everything in one place (app, 5 minute video, report, poster, code, data): https://warren-530.github.io/fire-harmony/hub.html

Report (47 pages, PDF): https://warren-530.github.io/fire-harmony/Fire_Harmony_report.pdf

· Code: https://github.com/Warren-530/fire-harmony

· Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/warrensaw530/fire-harmony

What it does

Fire Harmony gives the fire history of any place on Earth on one consistent scale. A user searches 4,329 countries, states and continent groups or 4,197 cities, draws a rectangle, polygon or circle, types coordinates, or clicks a hexagon on the map. For that area the app shows:

  • A burning calendar: every month since November 2000 as one box, coloured by the number of hotspots. The fire season, the bad years and this year stand out at once.
  • This month against normal: the anomaly against the median of 2001 to 2025, its rank among all years, and the year so far.
  • Any range of months: its total with a 90% range, its normal and its rank among the same months of every year. It also gives the busiest month and the raw detections of each satellite.
  • The trend and the critical period: a Mann Kendall test with Sen’s slope, and the months that usually burn worst, as CONAE defines them.
  • A map of tested trends: the trend view colours a hexagon red or blue only where its trend from 2001 to 2025 passes a 5% false discovery rate, and grey where it does not.
  • Why a month was unusual: how much of the fire anomaly the rain of the last three months and the heat explain. It also shows how El Niño moves the rain.
  • What comes next: the chance of above normal fire one, two and three months ahead, with its tested skill.
  • Downloads: the monthly record as CSV, the calendar and charts as pictures, and every satellite hotspot of the area and period as CSV.

The Dashboard shows every statistic of the project on one page. Its scope bar sets the place, or a circle of 50 km around a city, the years, the months and the scale, and every chart that can follow it does. Rankings puts all 4,330 places in one table: the world, 246 countries, 4,075 states and 8 continent groups (the six continents, Antarctica and the open ocean). It sorts by any column, filters by continent, country, trend and amount of fire, and uses the same tested verdict on each trend as the map. A Haze page links fires in Sumatra and Borneo to the air in 28 cities in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Brunei. A Methods page explains how the harmonization works and how we tested it.

On a phone the panel becomes a bottom sheet with three heights, so the map stays in view. Every view has its own link, so a shared link opens the same place, months and tab. The app has dark and light themes, and a command palette (Ctrl or Cmd and K).

Ask, from the header of every page, answers questions in plain words, such as how unusual a month was in a place or which countries have the fastest rising fire. A language model (Google Gemini, free tier) reads the question, but it can answer only with numbers it looks up through four tools that read the app’s own data, and every answer links to the places it used on the map.

How it works

  1. Data. We read all 640,601,590 NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). We checked our copy against official FIRMS files row by row: 100% match.
  2. Cleaning. One schema for every sensor, local solar time, one confidence rule, and vegetation fires only. A mask removes factories, gas flares, volcanoes and open water where NASA’s labels are missing.
  3. A grid of hexagons. We count hotspots on H3 hexagons of about 253 km², by month and satellite, for 413,699 hexagons.
  4. Harmonization. We scale the VIIRS satellites to NOAA-20 and average them, so more satellites never mean more fire. For the MODIS years, gradient boosting (LightGBM) predicts what NOAA-20 would have counted from what Terra and Aqua saw. We trained and scored it on years and regions it never saw. Every modelled value gets a 90% range.
  5. Tests. At the two sensor changes the record steps by 0.55% (2012) and 0.85% (2002), inside the spread of placebo tests at dates with no change (1.2% and 5.0%). ESA Fire_cci burned area agrees at the 2012 switch: against it, the record steps by 3.2%, where a naive join steps by 720%. On years and regions the model never saw, 92% to 96% of monthly totals fall inside their 90% range.
  6. Trends. A Mann Kendall test with Sen’s slope for every hexagon, country and state, with false discovery control at 5% across all of them. A second record built from MODIS alone, which never touches VIIRS, checks that the harmonization does not make the trends.
  7. Climate links. GPM IMERG rain, MERRA-2 weather and aerosols, GFWED fire weather and the ONI and DMI indices explain unusual months. They also feed the outlook and link fire to haze.
  8. The app. A pure frontend in React and TypeScript. DuckDB runs inside the browser and reads only the bytes it needs from static Parquet files. MapLibre and deck.gl draw the hexagons in 2D and 3D, and Observable Plot draws the charts. There is no server, no login, and nothing that sleeps.

What we found

  • No seams. The record steps by 0.55% in 2012 and 0.85% in 2002, smaller than the steps at dates when nothing changed.
  • Why one factor fails. At the same hour, Suomi NPP (VIIRS) counts 6.1 times the hotspots of Aqua (MODIS) but only 1.3 times the fire power: it sees the weak fires. In 9 hexagons out of 10 the rate lies between 4.1 and 13.5, so we use a model, not a factor.
  • Where fire changes. World fire fell by 6.3% per decade from 2001 to 2025, and by 11.0% in a record from MODIS alone, so the direction is surer than the size. Of the 7,449 level 3 hexagons with enough fire to test, 1,950 fell and 810 rose at a 5% false discovery rate: 2.4 falls for every rise. A record from MODIS alone has the same sign for 48 of the 49 countries with a significant trend.
  • What comes next. One month ahead, the outlook has a Brier skill score of 0.15 against a fixed 50% chance (95% range 0.11 to 0.17), on years it never saw; two and three months ahead the skill is small (0.06 and 0.04). It beats that chance on five of the six continents, but not in Africa. In October 2026, Central Kalimantan burned at 13.8 times its normal, and the outlook gives Indonesia an 84% chance of above normal fire in November, against a normal chance of 46%.
  • Haze. In Kuala Lumpur, 88% of the smoke comes from Sumatra. Beyond the usual rise of the season, fires upwind explain 55% of the ups and downs of its haze.

Benefits

  • For fire managers and early warning teams: the critical period of their area, how unusual this season is, and what the next three months may bring.
  • For scientists: a record they can use for trends from 2001 on the scale of VIIRS, not only from 2012, with tests and uncertainty for every value.
  • For planners: Rankings shows which places rise fastest and which burn far above normal now, with trends that are tested rather than guessed.
  • For the public and health agencies: the link between fires and haze, city by city.
  • For everyone: free, open, fast and in plain English, with colours that colour blind readers can tell apart.
  • Who runs it and who pays: the record and the app stay free, and they cost little to run because the app needs no server. A small team could keep them up to date, paid for by alerts or an API for plantations and insurers that need to know where fire runs far above normal.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, LightGBM, pyMannKendall, H3, xarray, Quarto and Typst for the pipeline and the report. React, Vite, TypeScript, DuckDB-WASM, MapLibre GL JS, deck.gl, h3-js and Observable Plot for the app, all open source. The Ask panel uses the Google Gemini API, through a small Google Apps Script relay.
